etymology: Through Old French sauveour from Latin salvator, one who saves. Webster 1828: one that saves or preserves; and, by way of eminence, Jesus Christ, who has opened the way to everlasting salvation. The KJV spelling with -our is retained here as the Authorized Version’s own.
biblical_def: In the Old Testament Saviour is a divine title with an exclusive claim attached to it. I, even I, am the LORD; and beside me there is no saviour (Isaiah 43:11), and again through Hosea, thou shalt know no god but me: for there is no saviour beside me (Hosea 13:4). The claim is not that God is the best of several rescuers but that there is no other of the kind. He is the LORD thy God, the Holy One of Israel, thy Saviour (Isaiah 43:3), and a God that hidest thyself, O God of Israel, the Saviour (Isaiah 45:15). Israel’s sin is stated as forgetting Him: They forgat God their saviour, which had done great things in Egypt (Psalm 106:21). The New Testament then applies the exclusive title to Jesus of Nazareth without hesitation or qualification: unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord (Luke 2:11); the Samaritans confess this is indeed the Christ, the Saviour of the world (John 4:42); and Paul joins the two words in one phrase, the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ (Titus 2:13). If Isaiah 43:11 is true, Titus 2:13 is a confession of the deity of Christ, and the two verses together are among the strongest arguments in Scripture for it.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SAVIOUR as one that saves or preserves; and adds that, by way of eminence, the appellation belongs to Jesus Christ, who has opened the way to everlasting salvation by His obedience and death.
webster_full: SAVIOUR, n. — One that saves or preserves; but properly applied only to Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, who has opened the way to everlasting salvation by his obedience and death, and who is therefore called the Saviour, by way of distinction, the Saviour of men, the Saviour of the world.
In the Old Testament the term is applied to men whom God raised up to deliver Israel, but always in a derived sense; the LORD Himself declares that beside Him there is no saviour.

Webster’s by way of distinction is the theological point. Where the word appears with the article and without qualification, it is a claim of exclusivity, and the New Testament makes that claim of Christ.
scriptures: Isaiah 43:11
I, even I, am the LORD; and beside me there is no saviour.
Isaiah 45:15
Verily thou art a God that hidest thyself, O God of Israel, the Saviour.
Hosea 13:4
Yet I am the LORD thy God from the land of Egypt, and thou shalt know no god but me: for there is no saviour beside me.
Luke 2:11
For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord.
Titus 2:13
Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ;
corruption_summary: The title is corrupted when it is generalized — a saviour figure among the world’s religions — and when it is severed from lordship, so that Christ is received as rescuer and refused as King.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 43:11 closes the question of religious pluralism before it is asked. Beside me there is no saviour is not a claim about Israel’s preference but about reality, and Hosea 13:4 repeats it. When the New Testament transfers the title to Jesus — and Peter states the consequence, neither is there salvation in any other (Acts 4:12) — it is not adding a rival to a crowded field; it is identifying the one Saviour of Isaiah. The modern proposal that Christ is one saviour figure among several, or that sincere devotion in any tradition reaches the same end, is not a development of Christianity but a denial of the sentence Isaiah wrote.

The second corruption is domestic. Luke 2:11 gives the title in a series: a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord. The angel does not offer the church a choice among them. Where the gospel is preached as rescue from consequences with the lordship of Christ postponed as an optional later step, the sentence has been broken in half. The Reformed answer is not that obedience earns salvation but that the Christ who saves is a whole Christ — prophet, priest, and king — and that a faith which receives Him as priest only has not laid hold of Him at all. The same Paul who wrote of the great God and our Saviour wrote in the next verse that He gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.
roots_summary: The Hebrew moshia' is the participle of the verb to save or deliver, the root behind the names Joshua and Jesus; the Greek soter is the standing New Testament title.
roots_lines: Hebrew yasha' (H3467) — to save, deliver, give victory; its participle moshia' is the saviour of Isaiah 43:11 and Hosea 13:4.
Hebrew Yehoshua — the LORD is salvation; the same root, and the Hebrew name behind Joshua and Jesus (Matthew 1:21).
Hebrew yeshu'ah (H3444) — salvation; the horn of my salvation (2 Samuel 22:3).
Greek soter (G4990) — saviour, deliverer; Luke 2:11, John 4:42, Titus 2:13, and repeatedly in the Pastoral Epistles of both the Father and the Son.
Titus 2:13 is governed by a single article in the Greek, joining the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ as one Person — a construction the Reformers pressed against Arian readings.
usage: Beside me there is no saviour (Isaiah 43:11) — exclusivity claimed by God for Himself.
A Saviour, which is Christ the Lord (Luke 2:11) — the three titles given together and not separately.
The great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ (Titus 2:13) — the Old Testament title applied to the incarnate Son.

etymology: From make, Old English macian. Webster 1828: the Creator; and, in a lower sense, one who makes or forms. Applied to God the word is a title of right — the one who made a thing has a claim on it — and the Authorized Version uses it where that claim is being pressed.
biblical_def: Maker in Scripture is a title that settles arguments. Eliphaz asks Job, shall a man be more pure than his maker? (Job 4:17), and Elihu will not flatter because my maker would soon take me away (Job 32:22). The psalm makes it the ground of worship: O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker (Psalm 95:6) — posture follows from origin. Proverbs makes it the ground of social duty, twice: He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker (Proverbs 14:31) and Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker (Proverbs 17:5). The reason is given plainly: The rich and poor meet together: the LORD is the maker of them all (Proverbs 22:2). Isaiah turns the title into the tenderest metaphor in the prophets: thy Maker is thine husband; the LORD of hosts is his name (Isaiah 54:5). And Hebrews sets it at the end of Abraham’s looking: he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God (Hebrews 11:10). The word therefore grounds worship, ethics, marriage, and hope in a single fact — that we did not make ourselves.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MAKER as the Creator — a title given to God by way of eminence — and, secondarily, one who forms, shapes, or fabricates anything. The theological weight lies in the right of the one who made.
webster_full: MAKER, n. — The Creator. God is called the Maker of all things, and the title belongs to Him by way of eminence.
One who makes, forms, shapes or moulds; a manufacturer; as, a maker of cloth.
One who writes verses; a poet — an older English sense, now obsolete.

Webster puts the divine sense first, and rightly. In English the word can name a craftsman, but in Scripture it names a right: the one who made a thing may dispose of it, and the creature owes Him worship because of what he is, not merely because of what he has received.
scriptures: Job 4:17
Shall mortal man be more just than God? shall a man be more pure than his maker?
Psalm 95:6
O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker.
Proverbs 14:31
He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker: but he that honoureth him hath mercy on the poor.
Isaiah 54:5
For thy Maker is thine husband; the LORD of hosts is his name; and thy Redeemer the Holy One of Israel; The God of the whole earth shall he be called.
Hebrews 11:10
For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
corruption_summary: The title is emptied by any account of origins that removes a Maker — and with Him the ground Proverbs gives for honouring the poor, since the argument there is not shared humanity in the abstract but a shared Maker.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 14:31 and 17:5 do not argue from dignity as a self-evident property. They argue from a Maker: to oppress or mock the poor is to reproach the One who made him. Remove the Maker and the argument has no premise left, whatever sentiment survives it. This is why the Christian case for the worth of every human being cannot be borrowed from the age’s vocabulary and must be preached from Genesis 1:27 and Proverbs 22:2. The rich and poor meet together: the LORD is the maker of them all is a sentence about creation before it is a sentence about ethics, and the ethics will not stand without it.

Psalm 95:6 shows the same structure in worship. The reason to kneel is that He is the LORD our maker, and the psalm goes on immediately to the warning about hardening the heart as at Meribah. Worship offered on any other ground — because it is meaningful, because it is moving, because it is our tradition — is worship resting on the worshipper. Isaiah 54:5 then adds the astonishment: the Maker is also the husband. The God who has the absolute right of a Creator over His creature has bound Himself to her by covenant, and the second fact does not cancel the first but makes it bearable.
roots_summary: The Hebrew is the participle 'oseh, the one making, from the ordinary verb to do or make; Isaiah 54:5 uses a plural of majesty. The Greek in Hebrews 11:10 is technites, a craftsman, paired with demiourgos.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'asah (H6213) — to do, make, fashion; its participle 'oseh gives maker (Job 4:17; Psalm 95:6; Proverbs 14:31).
Hebrew 'osayik in Isaiah 54:5 — a plural form, thy Makers, a plural of majesty the KJV renders as a singular Maker.
Hebrew bara' (H1254) — to create; used in Scripture only with God as subject, and standing behind the doctrine the title assumes.
Greek technites (G5079) — a craftsman, designer; whose builder and maker is God (Hebrews 11:10).
Greek demiourgos (G1217) — a maker, framer; the second noun in Hebrews 11:10, rendered maker.
usage: Let us kneel before the LORD our maker (Psalm 95:6) — the posture of worship argued from the fact of creation.
He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker (Proverbs 14:31) — social duty grounded in a shared origin.
Thy Maker is thine husband (Isaiah 54:5) — the Creator’s right joined to the Husband’s covenant.

etymology: Old English cwic, living, alive. Webster 1828 gives the primary sense as living, alive, and only afterward the derived sense of speed. The KJV uses the older meaning throughout — the quick and the dead means the living and the dead — and modern readers routinely mistake it.
biblical_def: In the Authorized Version quick means alive. The creed’s phrase comes straight from Scripture: Peter preaches that Christ was ordained of God to be the Judge of quick and dead (Acts 10:42); Paul charges Timothy before the Lord who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom (2 Timothy 4:1); and Peter writes of those that is ready to judge the quick and the dead (1 Peter 4:5). The phrase asserts two things at once — that Christ is Judge of all men, and that death does not remove a man from His jurisdiction. The older sense appears elsewhere. The rebels in Numbers go down quick into the pit, and the psalmist prays let them go down quick into hell (Psalm 55:15) and remembers that his enemies had swallowed us up quick (Psalm 124:3) — alive, not swiftly. The priestly law speaks of quick raw flesh in a leprous rising (Leviticus 13:10), living tissue exposed. And the messianic prophecy says of the Branch that God shall make him of quick understanding in the fear of the LORD (Isaiah 11:3), where the Hebrew idiom is a keen scent — a discernment that does not depend on the sight of the eyes.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives QUICK first as living; alive; not dead — citing the Scripture phrase the quick and the dead — and only then the familiar sense of swift or rapid. The KJV uses the primary, older meaning.
webster_full: QUICK, a. — Primarily, alive; living; opposed to dead or unanimated; as, the quick and the dead.
Swift; hasty; done with celerity; as, a quick return.
Speedy; done or occurring in a short time.
QUICK, n. — A living animal or plant; also, the living flesh; sensible parts; as, to cut to the quick.

The English idiom cut to the quick preserves the biblical sense exactly — to cut through the dead outer layer to the living flesh beneath — which is also the force of Hebrews 4:12, where the word of God is quick, and powerful.
scriptures: Leviticus 13:10
And the priest shall see him: and, behold, if the rising be white in the skin, and it have turned the hair white, and there be quick raw flesh in the rising;
Psalm 124:3
Then they had swallowed us up quick, when their wrath was kindled against us:
Isaiah 11:3
And shall make him of quick understanding in the fear of the LORD: and he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes, neither reprove after the hearing of his ears:
Acts 10:42
And he commanded us to preach unto the people, and to testify that it is he which was ordained of God to be the Judge of quick and dead.
2 Timothy 4:1
I charge thee therefore before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom;
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is a plain misreading: the quick and the dead taken as the fast and the dead, which empties the creedal phrase of the doctrine it was written to carry.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No movement has redefined quick; English simply moved on, and the archaic sense survives only in the creed and in the idiom cut to the quick. But the misreading has a doctrinal cost. The Judge of quick and dead asserts a universal jurisdiction that reaches across death itself, which is exactly why the phrase stands in the Apostles’ Creed and in the confessions. Read as a comment on speed, it says nothing at all.

The principle to recover is the general judgment. Acts 10:42, 2 Timothy 4:1, and 1 Peter 4:5 each attach the phrase to Christ’s appointment as Judge, and Paul preaches at Athens that God hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom he hath ordained (Acts 17:31). Both the living and the dead are raised and judged; there is no third category and no exemption for those already gone. And the doctrine is not bare terror for the believer, since the Judge is the same Christ who is also the Advocate — which is why Paul can charge Timothy by the coming judgment and in the same breath speak of the crown of righteousness laid up for him.
roots_summary: The Hebrew chay means living; the Greek zao is the participle of the verb to live. English quick is the native word for alive, displaced by the Latinate living and surviving now mostly in the creed.
roots_lines: Old English cwic — alive, living; the native English word, cognate with Latin vivus.
Hebrew chay (H2416) — living, alive; swallowed us up quick (Psalm 124:3), quick raw flesh (Leviticus 13:10).
Hebrew hariach in Isaiah 11:3 — literally his scenting, a keen discernment; the KJV renders it quick understanding.
Greek zao (G2198) — to live; the participle gives the quick in Acts 10:42, 2 Timothy 4:1, and 1 Peter 4:5.
The same Greek family gives Hebrews 4:12, the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword — living, not fast.
usage: The Judge of quick and dead (Acts 10:42) — the living and the dead; the creedal phrase in its biblical source.
Swallowed us up quick (Psalm 124:3) — alive, as the earth swallowed Korah.
Quick understanding in the fear of the LORD (Isaiah 11:3) — a discernment not dependent on sight or hearing.

etymology: From Latin divinus, belonging to a god. Webster 1828 gives the adjective — pertaining to the true God; proceeding from God — and a separate verb, to foretell or to practise divination. Both are in the Authorized Version, and they must not be confused: the adjective belongs to God, the verb to the diviner.
biblical_def: The KJV uses divine as two distinct words. As an adjective it marks what belongs to God: Hebrews describes the tabernacle order as ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary (Hebrews 9:1); Peter says his divine power hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness (2 Peter 1:3), and, most remarkably, that believers might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust (2 Peter 1:4). Proverbs uses it of a king’s judgment: A divine sentence is in the lips of the king (Proverbs 16:10) — an oracle, a weighty verdict. As a verb it means to practise divination, and Scripture condemns it wherever it is not merely reporting. Joseph says of his cup, wot ye not that such a man as I can certainly divine? (Genesis 44:15), speaking as an Egyptian ruler to brothers who do not know him. Ezekiel judges the false prophetesses: ye shall see no more vanity, nor divine divinations (Ezekiel 13:23), and the diviners of Jerusalem divine a lie unto thee (Ezekiel 21:29). The adjective and the verb sit a page apart and point in opposite directions — what proceeds from God, and what pretends to.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives DIVINE, adj., as pertaining to the true God, proceeding from Him, excellent in the highest degree; and DIVINE, v., as to foreknow, to foretell, to use or practise divination. The KJV employs both, and they are opposite in moral direction.
webster_full: DIVINE, a. [L. divinus.] — Pertaining to the true God; as, the divine nature; divine perfections.
Proceeding from God; as, divine judgments; divine grace.
Excellent in the highest degree; extraordinary; apparently above what is human.
DIVINE, v.t. — To foreknow; to foretell; to presage. To deify. To use or practise divination.
DIVINE, n. — A minister of the gospel; a theologian — the sense in which the Westminster and Baptist assemblies were composed of divines.
scriptures: Genesis 44:15
And Joseph said unto them, What deed is this that ye have done? wot ye not that such a man as I can certainly divine?
Proverbs 16:10
A divine sentence is in the lips of the king: his mouth transgresseth not in judgment.
Ezekiel 13:23
Therefore ye shall see no more vanity, nor divine divinations: for I will deliver my people out of your hand: and ye shall know that I am the LORD.
Hebrews 9:1
Then verily the first covenant had also ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary.
2 Peter 1:4
Whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust.
corruption_summary: 2 Peter 1:4 is the most abused verse in this family. Partakers of the divine nature is corrupted into deification of the creature — whether in Eastern theosis pressed past its limits, in the Word of Faith teaching that believers are little gods, or in the therapeutic notion of a divine spark within.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter’s own sentence sets the limits. Believers become partakers of the divine nature by these — that is, by the exceeding great and precious promises — and the immediate content is moral: having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust. What is imparted is holiness, a real participation in the moral likeness of God through regeneration and sanctification, not a share in His incommunicable being. God’s aseity, immutability, simplicity, and omnipotence are not distributable. The Creator-creature distinction is not abolished in glory; it is the permanent condition of the redeemed. Any reading that makes a Christian divine in essence has crossed the line Scripture will not cross, and the Word of Faith teaching that believers are gods in the same class as God is a plain heresy on this verse.

The verb runs the other way and is the age’s live temptation. Ezekiel 13 is God’s judgment on women who sewed pillows and prophesied out of their own hearts, and it ends with the promise that they shall divine divinations no more. The New Testament closes the canon and the office; there is no continuing gift by which a man may tell another the secret will of God for his life. Where modern prophetic ministries offer exactly that — a word about a marriage, a job, a move — the form of Ezekiel 13 has returned, however warm the intention. The believer’s guidance is the sufficient Scripture, the ordinary means of grace, wisdom, and the counsel of the church.
roots_summary: The Greek adjective is theios, belonging to God; the Hebrew verb behind the KJV’s divine is qasam, to practise divination, or nachash, to use enchantment. The English word carries both because Latin did.
roots_lines: Greek theios (G2304) — divine, belonging to God; divine power and divine nature (2 Peter 1:3-4), divine service (Hebrews 9:1).
Hebrew qesem (H7081) — divination; behind a divine sentence is in the lips of the king (Proverbs 16:10), where the KJV uses the noun of a weighty oracle.
Hebrew nachash (H5172) — to practise enchantment, to divine; Joseph’s words in Genesis 44:15.
Hebrew qasam (H7080) — to divine; nor divine divinations (Ezekiel 13:23), a cognate accusative the KJV preserves.
The English noun divine for a theologian gives the historic title of the Westminster Assembly of Divines, and is Webster’s fifth sense.
usage: Ordinances of divine service (Hebrews 9:1) — the adjective; worship ordered by God rather than by taste.
Partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4) — moral likeness through the promises, not deification of the creature.
Nor divine divinations (Ezekiel 13:23) — the verb; the practice God ends among His people.

etymology: From Latin tormentum, an instrument of torture, from torquere, to twist. Webster 1828: extreme pain; anguish; the utmost degree of misery, either of body or mind. In the Authorized Version the word belongs to the demons’ dread, to the rich man in Luke 16, and to the final state of those who refuse the gospel.
biblical_def: The demons use the word first, and they use it of themselves. What have we to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of God? art thou come hither to torment us before the time? (Matthew 8:29); the Gadarene cries I adjure thee by God, that thou torment me not (Mark 5:7). Two things follow: the demons know a time is appointed, and they know who will execute it. The clearest narrative use is our Lord’s own. The rich man in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off (Luke 16:23), and pleads that his brothers be warned lest they also come into this place of torment (Luke 16:28). Revelation states the duration without softening: the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night (Revelation 14:11), and the devil, the beast, and the false prophet shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever (Revelation 20:10). Babylon’s fall is measured by it (Revelation 18:7, 10). The one gentle use points the other way: There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment (1 John 4:18) — the believer’s dread of judgment is what love drives out.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TORMENT as extreme pain; anguish; the utmost degree of misery, either of body or mind; and, as a verb, to put to extreme pain or anguish. He notes the Scripture use of the future punishment of the wicked.
webster_full: TORMENT, n. [L. tormentum, from torqueo, to twist.] — Extreme pain; anguish; the utmost degree of misery, either of body or mind.
That which gives pain, vexation or misery.
TORMENT, v.t. — To put to extreme pain or anguish; to inflict excruciating pain and misery, either of body or mind.
The Latin root is an instrument of torture, and the English kept the severity. The KJV does not use the word lightly, and neither should a preacher.
scriptures: Matthew 8:29
And, behold, they cried out, saying, What have we to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of God? art thou come hither to torment us before the time?
Luke 16:23
And in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom.
Luke 16:28
For I have five brethren; that he may testify unto them, lest they also come into this place of torment.
Revelation 14:11
And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.
1 John 4:18
There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love.
corruption_summary: The doctrine these texts carry — eternal conscious punishment — is corrupted by annihilationism, which ends the torment in destruction, and by universalism, which ends it in restoration; both must set aside the plain duration Revelation states.
corruption_paragraphs: Annihilationism, or conditional immortality, holds that the lost are finally destroyed rather than punished without end, and it has gained ground among evangelicals in the last century. Revelation 14:11 is the text it must handle, and the handling is always the same: for ever and ever is read as the permanence of the outcome rather than the duration of the experience. But the verse adds they have no rest day nor night, which is a description of ongoing conscious experience, and Revelation 20:10 uses the identical phrase of the devil, whom no annihilationist supposes to be extinguished at the moment of sentence. The Lord Jesus, who spoke of hell more than anyone in Scripture, describes it as a place where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched (Mark 9:44).

Universalism runs the other way, holding that all are finally saved, and it must set aside Luke 16 in particular. The rich man is conscious, articulate, and in torment; Abraham tells him between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot (Luke 16:26). The gulf is fixed, and it is fixed in a parable told by the Saviour Himself. The pastoral answer is not to soften the doctrine but to preach it as the demons apparently understand it — there is a time appointed and a Judge appointed — and then to preach 1 John 4:18, where the fear that has torment is cast out by a love that came to bear it.
roots_summary: The Greek noun basanos originally named a touchstone for testing metal, then the rack, then torment itself; the verb basanizo is what the demons dread and what Revelation predicts.
roots_lines: Greek basanos (G931) — a touchstone, then torture, then torment; being in torments (Luke 16:23) and fear hath torment (1 John 4:18).
Greek basanizo (G928) — to torment, to test by torture; art thou come hither to torment us before the time? (Matthew 8:29).
Greek basanismos (G929) — torment as an ongoing state; the smoke of their torment (Revelation 14:11), the fear of her torment (Revelation 18:10).
Greek eis aionas aionon — unto ages of ages, the phrase the KJV renders for ever and ever, used of God’s own eternity in the same book.
Greek kolasis (G2851) — punishment; everlasting punishment in Matthew 25:46, set in parallel with life eternal by the same adjective.
usage: Art thou come hither to torment us before the time? (Matthew 8:29) — the demons know a time is appointed and who will keep it.
In hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments (Luke 16:23) — conscious experience after death, taught by Christ.
Fear hath torment (1 John 4:18) — the dread of judgment, cast out by perfect love.

etymology: From Old French reprove, from Latin reprobare, to disapprove. Webster 1828: blame expressed to the face; censure for a fault; reprehension. In Scripture it is one of the four uses for which the inspired word is profitable, and Proverbs makes a man’s response to it the measure of whether he is wise or brutish.
biblical_def: Reproof is correction spoken to a man’s face, and Scripture treats his answer to it as diagnostic. Wisdom cries in the street, Turn you at my reproof: behold, I will pour out my spirit unto you (Proverbs 1:23), and the refusal is what condemns: ye have set at nought all my counsel, and would none of my reproof (Proverbs 1:25); they despised all my reproof (Proverbs 1:30). The verdicts are blunt. Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish (Proverbs 12:1). He is in the way of life that keepeth instruction: but he that refuseth reproof erreth (Proverbs 10:17). He that regardeth reproof shall be honoured (Proverbs 13:18), and he that regardeth reproof is prudent (Proverbs 15:5). The man who has ruined himself says it too late: How have I hated instruction, and my heart despised reproof (Proverbs 5:12). Paul then makes reproof one of the four things the Scriptures are for: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness (2 Timothy 3:16). A ministry that will not reprove is using only three quarters of the Book.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines REPROOF as blame expressed to the face; censure for a fault; reprehension; and notes that it is milder than reproach and is intended for correction rather than injury.
webster_full: REPROOF, n. — Blame expressed to the face; censure for a fault; reprehension.
Reproof differs from reproach and rebuke in being more gentle, and it is generally intended for the correction of the offender rather than for his injury.

Webster’s distinction is worth keeping. Reproof aims at recovery. Proverbs pairs it constantly with instruction, and 2 Timothy 3:16 sets it between doctrine and correction — a man is taught, shown where he has gone wrong, set straight, and then trained in righteousness.
scriptures: Proverbs 1:23
Turn you at my reproof: behold, I will pour out my spirit unto you, I will make known my words unto you.
Proverbs 5:12
And say, How have I hated instruction, and my heart despised reproof;
Proverbs 12:1
Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish.
Proverbs 15:5
A fool despiseth his father's instruction: but he that regardeth reproof is prudent.
2 Timothy 3:16
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: Reproof is corrupted by a therapeutic culture that treats all correction as harm, so that the reprover is judged rather than the fault — and by a church that has quietly dropped one of the four uses 2 Timothy 3:16 names for Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 12:1 states the alternative without a middle term: a man either loves instruction or hates reproof and is brutish. The word is deliberately animal — a beast can be driven but not taught, because it cannot receive correction as a reason. Where the reigning assumption is that being told one is wrong is itself an injury, this proverb becomes unsayable and its whole pedagogy collapses. Scripture’s own safeguards against cruelty are real and specific: reproof is to be given in meekness (Galatians 6:1), an elder is not to be rebuked but entreated as a father (1 Timothy 5:1), and the reprover is warned to look to himself. But those are rules for how to reprove, not permissions to stop.

The second corruption is in the pulpit. 2 Timothy 3:16 lists four profits of the inspired word, and reproof is the second. A preaching ministry built entirely on encouragement has not made Scripture more useful; it has declined three quarters of what Paul says it is for, since correction and instruction in righteousness both presuppose that something was wrong. Paul’s very next sentence gives the charge: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine (2 Timothy 4:2) — and the longsuffering is commanded in the same breath as the reproof, not instead of it.
roots_summary: The Hebrew tokachath is correction or argument, from a root meaning to decide or adjudicate; the Greek elegmos in 2 Timothy 3:16 means a conviction, a bringing to light of what is wrong.
roots_lines: Hebrew tokachath (H8433) — correction, reproof, argument; the standing Proverbs term (Proverbs 1:23, 25, 30; 12:1; 15:5).
Hebrew yakach (H3198) — to decide, adjudge, reprove; the root, which is why reproof in Proverbs has a judicial flavour rather than a merely emotional one.
Greek elegmos (G1650) — conviction, reproof; profitable for doctrine, for reproof (2 Timothy 3:16).
Greek elegcho (G1651) — to convict, to expose, to reprove; the command of 2 Timothy 4:2 and John 16:8 of the Spirit’s work.
Greek epanorthosis (G1882) — correction, setting straight again; the third item in 2 Timothy 3:16, which follows reproof as the restoration follows the diagnosis.
usage: He that hateth reproof is brutish (Proverbs 12:1) — the response to correction distinguishes a man from a beast.
He that regardeth reproof is prudent (Proverbs 15:5) — prudence defined by teachability.
Profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction (2 Timothy 3:16) — reproof is one of four uses of the inspired word, not an optional register.

etymology: From Latin subjectio, a placing under, from sub plus jacere, to throw. Webster 1828: the act of subduing; the state of being under the power or authority of another. In the New Testament the Greek is a military word for ranking under, and it governs Christ’s dominion, the church’s order, and a man’s rule over his own body.
biblical_def: The New Testament uses subjection for an ordered placing under, and its widest use is christological. Hebrews quotes the eighth psalm: Thou hast put all things in subjection under his feet. For in that he put all in subjection under him, he left nothing that is not put under him. But now we see not yet all things put under him (Hebrews 2:8) — the dominion is granted, the visible fulfilment is not yet complete, and the writer resolves the tension by pointing to Jesus crowned with glory. The same chapter notes that unto the angels hath he not put in subjection the world to come (Hebrews 2:5). Then the ordered applications. Paul disciplines himself: I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway (1 Corinthians 9:27). An overseer must be one that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity (1 Timothy 3:4). Women are to learn in silence with all subjection in the assembly (1 Timothy 2:11), and wives are to be in subjection to your own husbands (1 Peter 3:1). And Paul refuses it where the gospel is at stake: To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you (Galatians 2:5).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SUBJECTION as the act of subduing; the act of bringing under the dominion of another; and the state of being under the power, control, and government of another. The Greek adds the idea of ordered rank rather than crushed resistance.
webster_full: SUBJECTION, n. — The act of subduing; the act of vanquishing and bringing under the dominion of another.
The state of being under the power, control and government of another; as, the safety of life, liberty and property consists in our subjection to the laws.

Webster’s second illustration is the biblical instinct. Subjection is not the opposite of freedom; a lawless society is not free. The New Testament word is drawn from military ranking — a soldier placed in his order — which is why it can be used of the Son to the Father without any thought of inferiority of being.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 9:27
But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.
Galatians 2:5
To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you.
1 Timothy 3:4
One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity;
Hebrews 2:8
Thou hast put all things in subjection under his feet. For in that he put all in subjection under him, he left nothing that is not put under him. But now we see not yet all things put under him.
1 Peter 3:1
Likewise, ye wives, be in subjection to your own husbands; that, if any obey not the word, they also may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives;
corruption_summary: Subjection is corrupted by egalitarian readings that treat every ordered relation as oppression, and equally by abusers who quote 1 Peter 3:1 while ignoring the verses that bind the husband — the first denies the order, the second denies its terms.
corruption_paragraphs: The creational order of headship and submission between husband and wife is taught in Genesis 2, argued from creation in 1 Corinthians 11:3-9, applied in Ephesians 5:22-33, and repeated by Peter in 1 Peter 3:1-7. The egalitarian reading treats these as culturally bound accommodations that the gospel itself overturns, usually appealing to Galatians 3:28. But Galatians 3:28 concerns standing before God in justification, not the abolition of created office, and Paul who wrote it also wrote 1 Timothy 2:11-15 and grounded it in the order of creation rather than in Ephesian custom. The dictionary’s reference standard on this is the biblical-order entry, and the treatment of egalitarianism as a corruption of the creational pattern is stated there.

The second corruption is more wicked and more common in practice. 1 Peter 3:1 is quoted at wives by men who never read to verse 7, where the husband is commanded to dwell with his wife according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, on pain of having his prayers hindered — nor to Ephesians 5:25, where he is told to love her as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it. Headship in Scripture is defined by a Husband who died. A man who uses these texts to demand and not to spend himself has inverted them, and the elders of a church are bound to say so. The same chapter that requires an overseer to have his children in subjection with all gravity (1 Timothy 3:4) disqualifies the striker and the brawler two verses earlier.
roots_summary: The Greek hupotasso is a military term meaning to arrange under, to rank beneath; its noun hupotage is the New Testament’s subjection. It denotes ordered place, not enforced defeat, except where the context is conquest.
roots_lines: Greek hupotasso (G5293) — to arrange under, to subordinate, to place in rank beneath; used of Christ’s dominion, of wives, of citizens, and of the Son to the Father in 1 Corinthians 15:28.
Greek hupotage (G5292) — subjection, subordination; learn in silence with all subjection (1 Timothy 2:11), subjection unto the gospel of Christ (2 Corinthians 9:13).
Greek doulagogeo (G1396) — to lead as a slave, to bring under control; bring it into subjection of Paul’s own body (1 Corinthians 9:27).
Hebrews 2:8 quotes Psalm 8:6 in the Septuagint, where hupotasso renders the Hebrew for putting under the feet.
The middle voice of hupotasso is used of the wife in 1 Peter 3:1 — a voluntary ranking of oneself, not a subjugation imposed.
usage: Thou hast put all things in subjection under his feet… But now we see not yet all things put under him (Hebrews 2:8) — the dominion granted and not yet visibly complete.
I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection (1 Corinthians 9:27) — the apostle’s own discipline, lest he be a castaway.
We gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour (Galatians 2:5) — where the gospel is at stake, subjection is refused outright.

etymology: From Latin resistere, to stand back or stand against. Webster 1828: to stand against; to withstand; to oppose. The Authorized Version uses it in four directions — Satan resisting the saints, men resisting the Holy Ghost, believers resisting the devil, and the prohibition against resisting the powers God has ordained.
biblical_def: Resist in Scripture is a word about who is standing against whom. Satan stands at Joshua’s right hand to resist him (Zechariah 3:1) — the accuser’s posture, opposed by the LORD who rebukes him. Stephen makes the terrible charge against the council: Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye (Acts 7:51). Paul says of the last-days deceivers, as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these also resist the truth (2 Timothy 3:8). The believer’s own commanded resistance is aimed at exactly one target, and it comes with a promise and a precondition: Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you (James 4:7). Two directions are forbidden. Personal retaliation: I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also (Matthew 5:39). And the civil order: Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation (Romans 13:2). Against that, God’s own resistance is aimed at one class of men: God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble (1 Peter 5:5).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines RESIST as to stand against; to withstand; to obstruct that which advances; to oppose. The Greek word behind the New Testament use is drawn from a battle line: to set oneself in array against.
webster_full: RESIST, v.t. [L. resisto; re and sisto, to stand.] — To stand against; to withstand; to obstruct that which comes or advances.
To oppose; to act in opposition, either by direct force or by counteracting means.
In Scripture, to withstand or oppose the Holy Spirit, that is, to reject His counsels and refuse obedience to His influence.

Webster’s third sense is Acts 7:51 exactly, and the theology behind it matters: men genuinely resist the outward call of the word and the striving of the Spirit, though the effectual call of the elect is not finally resisted.
scriptures: Zechariah 3:1
And he shewed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to resist him.
Matthew 5:39
But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.
Acts 7:51
Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye.
Romans 13:2
Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation.
James 4:7
Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
corruption_summary: Acts 7:51 is corrupted into a proof-text against the effectual call, as though grace were universally resistible in every sense; and James 4:7 is corrupted by the deliverance ministries that detach the resisting from the submitting which precedes it in the same verse.
corruption_paragraphs: Stephen says the council always resist the Holy Ghost, and Arminian readings take this as decisive against irresistible grace. The distinction the Reformed have always drawn is between the outward call, which comes through the preached word to all who hear and is constantly resisted, and the effectual call, by which the Spirit regenerates and draws the elect. Stephen’s hearers are resisting the first; nothing in the verse concerns the second. The doctrine is not that no man ever resists the Spirit — Scripture says plainly that men do, and Stephen was stoned by them — but that when God purposes to save a man, He gives a new heart, and the will that was unwilling becomes willing. Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power (Psalm 110:3).

James 4:7 is two commands in one sentence, and the modern deliverance industry has taken the second without the first. Submit yourselves therefore to God comes before Resist the devil, and the promise that he will flee is attached to the pair. Techniques of rebuking, binding, and commanding, practised by men whose lives are not submitted, have no warrant here. Nor does the verse license a Christian to go looking for the devil; the whole context is repentance, cleansing of hands, and purifying of hearts. Romans 13:2 sets the other boundary and it cuts against the age’s instinct: the ordinary duty of the Christian toward the civil power is submission, and only where the magistrate commands what God forbids does Peter’s we ought to obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29) apply.
roots_summary: The main Greek verb is anthistemi, to set oneself against, from a battle line; antitasso in James 4:7 and 1 Peter 5:5 is the same military tasso family that gives subjection, arranged against rather than under.
roots_lines: Greek anthistemi (G436) — to stand against, to withstand; resist the devil (James 4:7), resist the truth (2 Timothy 3:8), resisteth the power (Romans 13:2).
Greek antitasso (G498) — to arrange in battle against; God resisteth the proud (1 Peter 5:5; James 4:6).
Greek antipipto (G496) — to fall against, to rush against; ye do always resist the Holy Ghost (Acts 7:51).
Hebrew satan (H7853) — to be an adversary, to oppose; the verb behind Satan standing at his right hand to resist him (Zechariah 3:1).
The shared tasso root in antitasso and hupotasso is the New Testament’s picture of the two possible positions before God: ranked under, or arrayed against.
usage: Ye do always resist the Holy Ghost (Acts 7:51) — the outward call genuinely resisted, and the charge that cost Stephen his life.
Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil (James 4:7) — the order of the two commands is the condition of the promise.
God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble (1 Peter 5:5) — the one class God Himself stands against.

etymology: From upright, standing erect, and by transfer morally straight. Webster 1828: honestly; with strict observance of rectitude. Scripture’s adverb is almost always attached to walking, and the picture is of a straight line rather than a wandering one.
biblical_def: Uprightly in Scripture describes a manner of walking. The fifteenth psalm answers who may abide in God’s tabernacle with it: He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart (Psalm 15:2). The great promise is attached to it: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly (Psalm 84:11). Proverbs adds security: He that walketh uprightly walketh surely: but he that perverteth his ways shall be known (Proverbs 10:9), and protection: he is a buckler to them that walk uprightly (Proverbs 2:7). Its opposite is the perverse: Whoso walketh uprightly shall be saved: but he that is perverse in his ways shall fall at once (Proverbs 28:18). The word is also used of judging — do ye judge uprightly, O ye sons of men? (Psalm 58:1) and When I shall receive the congregation I will judge uprightly (Psalm 75:2) — and of speaking, in a verse that names the cost: They hate him that rebuketh in the gate, and they abhor him that speaketh uprightly (Amos 5:10). The straight walk is not always the safe one among men, whatever it is before God.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines UPRIGHTLY as in an erect position; and morally, honestly, with strict observance of rectitude. The KJV keeps the physical picture behind the moral sense: a straight walk, not a crooked one.
webster_full: UPRIGHTLY, adv. — In an erect position or posture.
Honestly; with strict observance of rectitude; as, to live uprightly.
UPRIGHT, a. — Erect; perpendicular. Adhering to rectitude; conformed to moral rectitude; honest; just.

The physical and the moral senses are one picture in Hebrew as in English. A man who walks a straight line arrives where he set out for; a man who walks crookedly arrives somewhere else, whatever he intended.
scriptures: Psalm 15:2
He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart.
Psalm 84:11
For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly.
Proverbs 2:7
He layeth up sound wisdom for the righteous: he is a buckler to them that walk uprightly.
Proverbs 10:9
He that walketh uprightly walketh surely: but he that perverteth his ways shall be known.
Amos 5:10
They hate him that rebuketh in the gate, and they abhor him that speaketh uprightly.
corruption_summary: Psalm 84:11 is corrupted by the prosperity teaching, which reads no good thing will he withhold as a guarantee of health and wealth for those who meet a condition — ignoring both what the verse names as the good things and what Amos 5:10 says happens to upright men.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 84:11 is a favourite of the prosperity preachers, and the verse itself refutes them. The good things it promises are named in the same sentence: the LORD will give grace and glory. The psalm is sung by a man who envies the sparrow for nesting near God’s altars and would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of his God than dwell in the tents of wickedness — it is not a formula for gain. And the condition, walking uprightly, is not a technique that obliges God but the ordinary description of a believer’s life. Where this verse is preached as a lever, both halves have been misread.

Amos 5:10 is the corrective that prosperity teaching cannot absorb: they hate him that rebuketh in the gate, and they abhor him that speaketh uprightly. Uprightness is frequently punished. The prophets were killed for it; our Lord was crucified for it; Stephen was stoned for it. The promise of Psalm 84:11 is real and it is eschatological in its weight — grace now, glory then, and nothing genuinely good withheld along the way — but it was never a promise of comfort in the gate. A church that has been taught to expect uprightness to be rewarded by men will not produce men who speak uprightly when it costs.
roots_summary: The Hebrew adverbs come from roots meaning whole, complete, or straight — tamim, blameless and whole, and yashar, straight or level. Both underlie the English upright.
roots_lines: Hebrew tamim (H8549) — complete, whole, blameless; he that walketh uprightly (Psalm 15:2; Proverbs 10:9), and the word describing Noah and required of sacrifices.
Hebrew yashar (H3477) — straight, level, right; behind speaketh uprightly (Amos 5:10) and judge uprightly (Psalm 75:2).
Hebrew tom (H8537) — integrity, completeness; the noun form, in the integrity of my heart.
The Hebrew tamim means whole rather than sinless; it describes a man undivided in his allegiance, which is why it can be predicated of David and Job.
Greek orthopodeo (G3716) — to walk straight; Paul’s charge at Antioch that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel (Galatians 2:14).
usage: He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness (Psalm 15:2) — the answer to who may abide in God’s tabernacle.
No good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly (Psalm 84:11) — the good things named in the verse are grace and glory.
They abhor him that speaketh uprightly (Amos 5:10) — the straight word is hated in the gate.

etymology: Old English tacen, a sign. Webster 1828: a sign; something intended to represent or indicate another thing or an event. In the Authorized Version the word is covenantal before it is anything else: the rainbow, circumcision, and the passover blood are all called tokens of a covenant.
biblical_def: A token in Scripture is a visible sign attached by God to a promise. After the flood He says three times over that the bow is one: This is the token of the covenant which I make between me and you and every living creature (Genesis 9:12); I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth (Genesis 9:13); This is the token of the covenant, which I have established between me and all flesh (Genesis 9:17). Circumcision is the same: ye shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin; and it shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you (Genesis 17:11). The exodus deliverance is bound on the hand and the forehead for a token upon thine hand, and for frontlets between thine eyes (Exodus 13:16). Rahab asks the spies for a true token that her house will be spared (Joshua 2:12), and receives the scarlet line. David prays, Shew me a token for good; that they which hate me may see it (Psalm 86:17). The New Testament keeps the word for a sign that reads two ways at once: the courage of a persecuted church is to them an evident token of perdition, but to you of salvation, and that of God (Philippians 1:28). And the darkest use is Judas’s kiss, a token agreed in advance (Mark 14:44).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TOKEN as a sign; something intended to represent or indicate another thing or an event; a mark; and, in a second sense, a memorial of friendship, an evidence of affection.
webster_full: TOKEN, n. — A sign; something intended to represent or indicate another thing or an event; as, the rainbow is a token of God’s covenant.
A mark; as, the tokens of a disease.
A memorial of friendship; something by which the friendship of another person is to be kept in mind.
Webster’s first illustration is Genesis 9 itself. The token is not the covenant; it is the sign appointed to it, and its whole force comes from the word of the God who appointed it.
scriptures: Genesis 9:13
I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth.
Genesis 17:11
And ye shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin; and it shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you.
Exodus 13:16
And it shall be for a token upon thine hand, and for frontlets between thine eyes: for by strength of hand the LORD brought us forth out of Egypt.
Psalm 86:17
Shew me a token for good; that they which hate me may see it, and be ashamed: because thou, LORD, hast holpen me, and comforted me.
Philippians 1:28
And in nothing terrified by your adversaries: which is to them an evident token of perdition, but to you of salvation, and that of God.
corruption_summary: The token is corrupted when the sign is severed from the word that appointed it — a rainbow made into a symbol of something God never attached to it, and covenant signs treated as either empty pictures or as conveying grace by the act itself.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 9 says three times what the bow means, and it means what God said. It is the token of a covenant that He will not again destroy the earth by a flood, and He states that the bow is set there so that I will look upon it, that I may remember the everlasting covenant. The sign points at God’s memory, not at ours, and it belongs to His promise and not to any human cause. To take the same arc and attach a different meaning to it — to make it the emblem of a movement whose defining claim is that Genesis 1:27 and 2:24 do not bind — is to take a covenant sign and hang another covenant on it. The dictionary states this plainly rather than obliquely: the bow is God’s, and its meaning was fixed before any of us arrived.

The second corruption is sacramental and runs in two directions. Circumcision was a token of the covenant, and Paul says of Abraham that he received it as a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised (Romans 4:11) — sign and seal of a righteousness already possessed by faith, not the means of obtaining it. Rome’s error is to make the sign convey grace by the working of the work; bare memorialism’s error is to make it a picture with nothing in it. The Reformed position holds both: baptism and the Lord’s Supper are signs and seals in which Christ is truly present to the believer by faith, and empty to the one who comes without it.
roots_summary: The Hebrew is 'oth, a sign, the same word used of the signs in Egypt and of the sabbath; the Greek endeixis in Philippians 1:28 means a demonstration or proof shown forth.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'oth (H226) — a sign, token, mark; the rainbow (Genesis 9:12-17), circumcision (Genesis 17:11), the sabbath (Exodus 31:13).
Hebrew 'oth emeth — a true token; what Rahab asks of the spies (Joshua 2:12), answered by the scarlet line.
Hebrew mopheth (H4159) — a wonder or sign; often paired with 'oth in the exodus narratives.
Greek endeixis (G1732) — a showing forth, demonstration, proof; an evident token of perdition (Philippians 1:28).
Greek semeion (G4592) — a sign; the standard New Testament word, and the term John uses for the miracles of Christ.
usage: It shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth (Genesis 9:13) — the meaning of the bow is fixed by the God who set it.
A token of the covenant betwixt me and you (Genesis 17:11) — circumcision as sign and seal, not as the means of righteousness.
An evident token of perdition, but to you of salvation (Philippians 1:28) — one sign read two ways, and God is the one who gives it.
